etymology: From Anglo-Saxon stream, a current of water. Webster 1828: a current of water or other fluid; a river or brook. Amos demands that righteousness run like one, and Daniel sees a stream of fire proceeding from the throne.
biblical_def: Amos gives the prophets’ most quoted demand, and the figure is deliberately hydraulic: But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream (Amos 5:24). The verse comes immediately after God says He hates their feast days and will not accept their offerings; the stream is what He wants instead of a religion of assemblies without justice. Daniel sees the throne room and the stream there is fire: A fiery stream issued and came forth from before him: thousand thousands ministered unto him... the judgment was set, and the books were opened (Daniel 7:10). Our Lord uses a stream to test two houses: when the flood arose, the stream beat vehemently upon that house, and could not shake it: for it was founded upon a rock (Luke 6:48). The two houses look identical until the stream comes; the difference is invisible and underground. And Job turns the figure into a complaint about friends who fail in the dry season: My brethren have dealt deceitfully as a brook, and as the stream of brooks they pass away (Job 6:15).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines STREAM as a current of water or other fluid; a river, brook or rivulet; anything flowing continuously; a current of anything.
webster_full: STREAM, n. — A current of water or other fluid; a river, brook, or rivulet.
A current; a flow of anything; as a stream of light.
Anything issuing from a source and flowing continuously.
STREAM, v.i. — To flow; to move or run in a continuous current.
Anglo-Saxon stream; compare German Strom.
scriptures: Amos 5:24
But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.
Daniel 7:10
A fiery stream issued and came forth from before him: thousand thousands ministered unto him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him: the judgment was set, and the books were opened.
Luke 6:48

He is like a man which built an house, and digged deep, and laid the foundation on a rock: and when the flood arose, the stream beat vehemently upon that house, and could not shake it: for it was founded upon a rock.
Job 6:15
My brethren have dealt deceitfully as a brook, and as the stream of brooks they pass away;
corruption_summary: Amos 5:24 is one of the most-quoted verses in modern political preaching, and its immediate context — God’s rejection of a nation’s worship — is almost always dropped.
corruption_paragraphs: Let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream is regularly cited as a free-standing slogan for social causes, detached from the paragraph it concludes. Amos 5:21-23 is God saying He hates and despises their feast days, will not smell in their solemn assemblies, will not accept their burnt offerings, and commands them to take away the noise of their songs. The verse is therefore not a call to substitute activism for worship; it is a judgment on worship offered by people who were oppressing the poor and taking bribes in the gate, and a demand that the same God be obeyed in both. Detached from that setting, the verse can be made to serve almost any programme, which is precisely how it is generally used. The biblical categories in view are Amos’s own: the just balance, the honest court, the widow and the poor — not an autonomous political framework imported and then given a text.

Luke 6:48 is worth pressing for what it says about invisible foundations. The two builders in the parable produce houses that look the same; the difference is that one dug deep and laid a foundation on rock. That difference cannot be seen from the road and is not tested until the stream comes. Our Lord identifies the digging with hearing His sayings and doing them (Luke 6:47), which makes obedience the foundation-work rather than the decoration. This is not works-righteousness — the parable concerns the reality of discipleship, not the ground of justification — but it does mean that a profession untested by a stream has proved nothing about itself yet.
roots_summary: Hebrew nachal (H5158), a torrent or wadi; ethan (H386), perennial, ever-flowing; Aramaic nehar (H5103), a river; Greek potamos (G4215), a river or flood.
roots_lines: Hebrew nachal (H5158) — a torrent-valley or wadi, dry in summer; as the stream of brooks they pass away (Job 6:15).
Hebrew ethan (H386) — perennial, ever-flowing; a mighty stream in Amos 5:24 is a stream that does not fail in the dry season.
Aramaic nehar (H5103) — a river; a fiery stream issued (Daniel 7:10).
Greek potamos (G4215) — a river or flood; the stream that beat upon the house (Luke 6:48).
Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment, justice; the companion term to righteousness in Amos 5:24.
usage: Let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream (Amos 5:24) — and the verses before it reject the nation’s worship.
A fiery stream issued and came forth from before him (Daniel 7:10) — the throne room, and the books opened.
The stream beat vehemently upon that house, and could not shake it (Luke 6:48) — the difference was invisible until the stream came.

etymology: From Anglo-Saxon blaec, dark, of the darkest colour. Webster 1828: of the colour of night; destitute of light; dark. Scripture uses it of skin without disparagement, of a horse of famine, and of heavens that mourn.
biblical_def: The Song of Solomon opens with a woman describing herself without apology and without shame: I am black, but comely, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, as the tents of Kedar, as the curtains of Solomon (Song of Solomon 1:5), the next verse explaining that the sun had looked upon her because her brothers had made her keeper of the vineyards. Job uses the word of a body wrecked by disease: My skin is black upon me, and my bones are burned with heat (Job 30:30). In Revelation the third seal brings a black horse whose rider carries a balance, and the voice that follows prices wheat and barley at a day’s wage for a day’s food: I beheld, and lo a black horse; and he that sat on him had a pair of balances in his hand (Revelation 6:5). Our Lord uses the colour to prove how little a man governs: Neither shalt thou swear by thy head, because thou canst not make one hair white or black (Matthew 5:36) — the argument against oaths is that the swearer has nothing of his own to pledge.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines BLACK as of the colour of night; destitute of light; dark; and figuratively, dismal, gloomy, sullen, or wicked.
webster_full: BLACK, a. — Of the colour of night; destitute of light; dark.
Dark; dismal; gloomy; sullen; as a black day.
Sullenly angry; as a black look.
BLACK, n. — That which is destitute of light or whiteness; the darkest colour.
Anglo-Saxon blaec, black; distinguish the related blac, pale or shining.
scriptures: Song of Solomon 1:5
I am black, but comely, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, as the tents of Kedar, as the curtains of Solomon.
My skin is black upon me, and my bones are burned with heat.
Revelation 6:5
And when he had opened the third seal, I heard the third beast say, Come and see. And I beheld, and lo a black horse; and he that sat on him had a pair of balances in his hand.
Matthew 5:36
Neither shalt thou swear by thy head, because thou canst not make one hair white or black.
corruption_summary: Scripture’s use of black for skin carries no disparagement whatever, and the attempt to enlist the Bible for racial hierarchy has always required doing violence to its plain text.
corruption_paragraphs: The bride of the Song says I am black, but comely, and the following verse gives the cause — the sun had looked upon her because she had been set to keep vineyards. The text records a fact about complexion and immediately calls her beautiful; there is no hierarchy in it. The Bible’s anthropology forecloses any such hierarchy at the root: all men are of one blood (Acts 17:26), all descend from one Adam and share original sin (Romans 5:12), and all who are in Christ are one (Galatians 3:28). The so-called curse of Ham, long misused to justify slavery, is not in the text at all — Genesis 9:25 curses Canaan, not Ham, and concerns a people in the land, not a race. The dictionary names that misreading as the corruption it is.

Having said that, the biblical answer to racial hierarchy is not the modern framework that replaces it. Critical race theory and the antiracist frameworks built on it substitute an oppressor-oppressed binary based on race for the biblical categories of sin, the fallen heart, and covenant. That is a competing anthropology, not a development of the Christian one, and it cannot deliver what it promises because it has no doctrine of forgiveness and no category for a guilt that is actually removed. Scripture’s account is more radical in both directions: every man is guilty in Adam, and every man in Christ is one new man. Revelation 7:9 shows the outcome — a great multitude of all nations and kindreds and people and tongues before the throne.
roots_summary: Hebrew shachor (H7838), black; shachar (H7835), to be black or dusky; Greek melas (G3189), black; the root of English melancholy and melanin.
roots_lines: Hebrew shachor (H7838) — black, dusky; I am black, but comely (Song of Solomon 1:5).
Hebrew shachar (H7835) — to be black or grow dark; my skin is black upon me (Job 30:30).
Greek melas (G3189) — black; the third horse of Revelation 6:5 and the hair of Matthew 5:36.
Hebrew Qedar (H6938) — Kedar, whose tents were of dark goats’ hair; the bride’s comparison.
Greek zugos (G2218) — a yoke or balance; carried by the rider of the black horse, a symbol of scarcity.
usage: I am black, but comely (Song of Solomon 1:5) — a fact of complexion, and beauty affirmed in the same breath.
Lo a black horse; and he that sat on him had a pair of balances (Revelation 6:5) — famine, rationed by weight.
Thou canst not make one hair white or black (Matthew 5:36) — the swearer has nothing of his own to pledge.

etymology: From Anglo-Saxon botm, the lowest part. Webster 1828: the lowest part of anything; the ground under water; a valley or dale. Exodus sends Pharaoh’s host to the bottom as a stone, and Micah sends Israel’s sins to the same place.
biblical_def: The Song of the Sea uses the word for the finality of a judgment: The depths have covered them: they sank into the bottom as a stone (Exodus 15:5). Stones do not float, drift, or come back; the simile is chosen for its irreversibility, and Micah later applies the same geography to sin: God will cast all their sins into the depths of the sea (Micah 7:19). The word also names a low place in a landscape, and Zechariah’s first vision is set in one: behold a man riding upon a red horse, and he stood among the myrtle trees that were in the bottom (Zechariah 1:8) — a rider among low trees in a hollow, and the vision goes on to declare that the LORD is jealous for Jerusalem. Solomon’s chariot is described from its base upward: He made the pillars thereof of silver, the bottom thereof of gold, the covering of it of purple (Song of Solomon 3:10). And Jonah, praying from the fish, reports the lowest point a man has reached in Scripture: he went down to the bottoms of the mountains (Jonah 2:6).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines BOTTOM as the lowest part of anything; the ground under any body of water; a low ground or valley; the foundation or base.
webster_full: BOTTOM, n. — The lowest part of anything; as the bottom of a well.
The ground under any body of water; as the bottom of the sea.
A low ground; a valley; a dale.
The foundation or ground work of anything; the base.
Anglo-Saxon botm; compare German Boden, ground.
scriptures: Exodus 15:5
The depths have covered them: they sank into the bottom as a stone.
Zechariah 1:8
I saw by night, and behold a man riding upon a red horse, and he stood among the myrtle trees that were in the bottom; and behind him were there red horses, speckled, and white.
Song of Solomon 3:10
He made the pillars thereof of silver, the bottom thereof of gold, the covering of it of purple, the midst thereof being paved with love, for the daughters of Jerusalem.
Micah 7:19
He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.
corruption_summary: Micah 7:19 says God casts sins into the depths of the sea, which is a statement about their removal from His reckoning — not, as the therapeutic reading has it, about the believer’s feelings toward himself.
corruption_paragraphs: Thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea. The subject of the verb is God, and the action is judicial: the sins are removed from His account against His people. Micah has just asked Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity, and the whole passage is about the character of the Pardoner rather than the state of the pardoned man’s emotions. This matters because the verse is commonly deployed as an instruction to stop feeling bad, which is a different claim and a weaker one. The Reformed doctrine of justification supplies the actual comfort: the sin is not merely forgotten but paid, borne by a Substitute, and God is just in remitting it (Romans 3:26). A guilt removed on those terms is genuinely gone, and the believer’s peace rests on the transaction rather than on his success in not thinking about it.

Exodus 15:5 should not be softened either. The Song of the Sea is a victory hymn celebrating the drowning of an army, and it is sung by people who had watched it happen after four hundred years of bondage. Modern readers, taught to find such songs distasteful, generally handle them by treating the language as hyperbole or the theology as primitive. Scripture treats the event as a real judgment on a real oppressor who had drowned Hebrew infants (Exodus 1:22) and hardened himself through ten warnings. The same God who casts sins into the depths cast Pharaoh’s chariots there, and Revelation 15:3 puts the song of Moses in the mouths of the redeemed at the end. Mercy and judgment are not rival attributes to be balanced; they meet at the cross.
roots_summary: Hebrew metsolah (H4688), a depth or deep place; yarek (H3411), the recesses or base; metsullah (H4699), a shady bottom or hollow; yam (H3220), the sea.
roots_lines: Hebrew metsolah (H4688) — a depth, the deep of the sea; they sank into the bottom as a stone (Exodus 15:5).
Hebrew metsullah (H4699) — a shady place or hollow; the bottom where the myrtle trees stood (Zechariah 1:8).
Hebrew yarek (H3411) — the flank, the recesses, the lowest part; the bottoms of the mountains (Jonah 2:6).
Hebrew rephidah (H7507) — a support or base; the bottom thereof of gold (Song of Solomon 3:10).
Hebrew kabash (H3533) — to subdue, to tread down; he will subdue our iniquities (Micah 7:19).
usage: They sank into the bottom as a stone (Exodus 15:5) — the simile chosen for its irreversibility.
Thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea (Micah 7:19) — a judicial removal, God the actor.
Among the myrtle trees that were in the bottom (Zechariah 1:8) — a rider in a hollow, and a word of jealousy for Jerusalem.

etymology: From Latin largus, abundant, plentiful, bountiful, through French large. Webster 1828: big; of great size; wide; extensive; also liberal, abundant. In the Psalms deliverance is repeatedly described as being brought into a large place.
biblical_def: David’s standing image for rescue is not escape but room: He brought me forth also into a large place; he delivered me, because he delighted in me (Psalm 18:19). The trouble he was in was constriction — the snares of death, the floods of ungodly men — and the deliverance is space. He uses the figure again: hast not shut me up into the hand of the enemy: thou hast set my feet in a large room (Psalm 31:8). Nehemiah uses the word of a city that had walls and no people: Now the city was large and great: but the people were few therein, and the houses were not builded (Nehemiah 7:4) — a rebuilt wall around an empty city, which is why the next chapters concern the reading of the law and the repopulating of Jerusalem. Mark records the room prepared for the last supper: he will shew you a large upper room furnished and prepared: there make ready for us (Mark 14:15). And Paul draws attention to his own handwriting: Ye see how large a letter I have written unto you with mine own hand (Galatians 6:11).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines LARGE as big; of great size; bulky; wide; extensive; abundant; plentiful; and, of the heart or hand, liberal and generous.
webster_full: LARGE, a. — Big; of great size; bulky; as a large body.
Wide; extensive; as a large field or country.
Abundant; plentiful; ample; as a large supply of provisions.
Liberal; of a great or generous disposition; as a large heart.
AT LARGE, without restraint or confinement; also, fully, in the full extent. Latin largus, bountiful.
scriptures: Psalm 18:19
He brought me forth also into a large place; he delivered me, because he delighted in me.
Psalm 31:8
And hast not shut me up into the hand of the enemy: thou hast set my feet in a large room.
Nehemiah 7:4
Now the city was large and great: but the people were few therein, and the houses were not builded.
Mark 14:15
And he will shew you a large upper room furnished and prepared: there make ready for us.
corruption_summary: Psalm 18:19 grounds deliverance in God’s delight rather than the sufferer’s performance, and the clause because he delighted in me is the half most often left off.
corruption_paragraphs: He delivered me, because he delighted in me. The reason given for the rescue is not David’s merit but God’s pleasure in him, and the psalm has just described a deliverance in which David did nothing but cry out. The clause is the Old Testament in miniature of what the New Testament calls election according to the good pleasure of His will (Ephesians 1:5). Where it is dropped, Psalm 18 becomes a promise that God rescues those who have earned it, and the reader is left auditing his own life for the qualification. The verse does not describe a transaction; it describes a Father’s delight, and the following verses about David’s cleanness are the fruit of that relationship, not its price. Distinguishing the ground from the fruit is the difference between assurance and anxiety.

Nehemiah 7:4 is a quiet warning about the difference between structures and people. The wall was finished, the gates hung, the city large and great — and the people were few and the houses unbuilt. Nehemiah’s response occupies the rest of the book: the law read publicly from morning until midday, the people weeping and then commanded to rejoice, a covenant renewed in writing, and lots cast to bring one in ten to dwell in Jerusalem. The building programme was not the reformation; it was the precondition. Churches that have completed a construction project and find themselves large and empty are at Nehemiah 7:4, and the chapters that follow are the ones to read.
roots_summary: Hebrew merchab (H4800), a broad or roomy place; rachab (H7342), wide, broad; gadol (H1419), great; Greek megas (G3173), great, large; pelikos (G4080), how large.
roots_lines: Hebrew merchab (H4800) — a broad place, room; he brought me forth also into a large place (Psalm 18:19) and a large room (Psalm 31:8).
Hebrew rachab (H7342) — wide, broad, spacious; the city was large and great (Nehemiah 7:4).
Greek megas (G3173) — great, large; a large upper room (Mark 14:15).
Greek pelikos (G4080) — how great or how large; how large a letter (Galatians 6:11).
Hebrew chaphets (H2654) — to delight in, to take pleasure in; the reason given for the deliverance (Psalm 18:19).
usage: He brought me forth also into a large place (Psalm 18:19) — deliverance described as room, not escape.
Thou hast set my feet in a large room (Psalm 31:8) — the same figure, against being shut up.
The city was large and great: but the people were few therein (Nehemiah 7:4) — a finished wall around an empty city.

etymology: From Old French entree, from Latin intrare, to go in. Webster 1828: the passage by which persons enter a house; the act of entering. In the prophets the entry of a gate is where the decisive thing stands — an image of jealousy, or a call to wisdom.
biblical_def: Ezekiel, carried in vision to Jerusalem, is told to look and is shown what stands at the way in: behold northward at the gate of the altar this image of jealousy in the entry (Ezekiel 8:5). The idol is not hidden in a back chamber; it is at the entry, the first thing met, and the chapter goes on to greater abominations within. Where a thing is placed is part of what it means. Wisdom, by contrast, takes her stand at the same kind of place and calls aloud: She crieth at the gates, at the entry of the city, at the coming in at the doors (Proverbs 8:3) — not in the schools but at the traffic, where ordinary people pass. Jeremiah is sent to a specific gate to break a bottle and pronounce a judgment: go forth unto the valley of the son of Hinnom, which is by the entry of the east gate (Jeremiah 19:2). And Kings records a king dismantling the temple approaches to please a foreign power: the king's entry without, turned he from the house of the LORD for the king of Assyria (2 Kings 16:18).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ENTRY as the passage by which persons enter a house or other building; the act of entering; ingress; also the act of recording or setting down in writing.
webster_full: ENTRY, n. — The passage by which persons enter a house or other building.
The act of entering; ingress; as the entry of a person into a house.
The act of taking possession of lands or tenements.
The act of committing to writing, or of recording in a book.
Old French entree, from Latin intrare, to enter, from intra, within.
scriptures: Ezekiel 8:5

Then said he unto me, Son of man, lift up thine eyes now the way toward the north. So I lifted up mine eyes the way toward the north, and behold northward at the gate of the altar this image of jealousy in the entry.
Proverbs 8:3
She crieth at the gates, at the entry of the city, at the coming in at the doors.
Jeremiah 19:2
And go forth unto the valley of the son of Hinnom, which is by the entry of the east gate, and proclaim there the words that I shall tell thee,
2 Kings 16:18
And the covert for the sabbath that they had built in the house, and the king's entry without, turned he from the house of the LORD for the king of Assyria.
corruption_summary: 2 Kings 16:18 records a king altering the house of the LORD to accommodate a foreign power, and the alteration was architectural before it was theological.
corruption_paragraphs: Ahaz had already sent the silver and gold of the temple to Tiglath-pileser and had copied a Damascus altar for the temple court; here he removes the sabbath covert and the king’s outer entry for the king of Assyria. Nothing in the verse is presented as doctrinal reform. It is a rearrangement of approaches to suit an audience whose approval was needed, and the theology followed the furniture. The pattern is worth naming because it is the ordinary sequence of compromise in a church: the arrangement of the service, the placement of the pulpit and the table, what is said at the door and what is left unsaid, all adjusted for the sake of a hearer whose favour is wanted — and doctrine settles afterward into the shape of the room. The regulative principle of worship exists to prevent exactly this drift.

Proverbs 8:3 sets wisdom where the traffic is. She does not wait to be sought in a lecture hall; she cries at the gates, at the entry of the city, at the coming in at the doors, where the commerce and the courts and the ordinary business of the town went on. This bears on how the church conceives of its teaching. The wisdom literature assumes an audience of tradesmen, farmers, wives and young men, and addresses them where they are without lowering what it says. That is a different thing from the modern instinct to simplify by subtraction. Wisdom stands in the gate and speaks of righteousness, of the fear of the LORD, and of her own presence at the creation — the highest matter in the book — to whoever is passing.
roots_summary: Hebrew mabo (H3996), an entrance or coming in; pethach (H6607), an opening or doorway; shaar (H8179), a gate; Greek eisodos (G1529), an entrance.
roots_lines: Hebrew mabo (H3996) — an entrance, a coming in; at the entry of the city (Proverbs 8:3) and the king’s entry (2 Kings 16:18).
Hebrew pethach (H6607) — an opening or doorway; this image of jealousy in the entry (Ezekiel 8:5).
Hebrew shaar (H8179) — a gate, the place of counsel, court and commerce in an Israelite city.
Hebrew qinah (H7068) — jealousy or zeal; the name given to the idol at the entry (Ezekiel 8:5).
Greek eisodos (G1529) — an entrance or way in; the New Testament counterpart term.
usage: This image of jealousy in the entry (Ezekiel 8:5) — not hidden in a back chamber but at the way in.
She crieth at the gates, at the entry of the city (Proverbs 8:3) — wisdom standing where the traffic is.
The king's entry without, turned he from the house of the LORD for the king of Assyria (2 Kings 16:18) — the furniture moved first.

etymology: From Anglo-Saxon sceotan, to dart or send forth swiftly. Webster 1828: to let fly and drive with force, as an arrow from a bow. The Psalms use it of the wicked ambushing the upright, of God answering them in kind, and of a gesture of contempt made at the cross.
biblical_def: Psalm 11 describes the tactic of the wicked with precision, and the operative word is privily: lo, the wicked bend their bow, they make ready their arrow upon the string, that they may privily shoot at the upright in heart (Psalm 11:2). Preparation, concealment, and a specific target. Psalm 64 answers with the same verb turned round, and the reversal is exact: But God shall shoot at them with an arrow; suddenly shall they be wounded (Psalm 64:7) — they prepared in secret and God is sudden. The word also names a gesture. In the psalm our Lord quoted from the cross, the mockers do something with the mouth that is hard to render and easy to picture: All they that see me laugh me to scorn: they shoot out the lip, they shake the head (Psalm 22:7) — and Matthew 27:39 records the head-shaking at Calvary. Jonathan uses the word for the signal that saved David’s life: I will shoot three arrows on the side thereof, as though I shot at a mark (1 Samuel 20:20).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SHOOT as to let fly and drive with force; to discharge, as an arrow or a bullet; to send out or forth; to push out, as a bud or branch.
webster_full: SHOOT, v.t. — To let fly and drive with force; as, to shoot an arrow.
To discharge and cause to be driven with violence; as, to shoot a gun.
To send out or forth; to emit; as, to shoot forth rays.
SHOOT, v.i. — To germinate; to bud; to sprout; to push out, as a plant.
Anglo-Saxon sceotan, to dart forth — the root of shot, sheet and shut.
scriptures: Psalm 11:2
For, lo, the wicked bend their bow, they make ready their arrow upon the string, that they may privily shoot at the upright in heart.
Psalm 64:7
But God shall shoot at them with an arrow; suddenly shall they be wounded.
Psalm 22:7
All they that see me laugh me to scorn: they shoot out the lip, they shake the head, saying,
1 Samuel 20:20
And I will shoot three arrows on the side thereof, as though I shot at a mark.
corruption_summary: Psalm 22 is quoted by Christ from the cross and its details are fulfilled at Calvary, which the critical habit of treating messianic psalms as retrofitted after the fact cannot honestly explain.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 22 opens with the words our Lord cried from the cross and proceeds through a series of details the Gospels record: the mocking and head-shaking (Psalm 22:7; Matthew 27:39), the taunt He trusted on the LORD that he would deliver him (Psalm 22:8; Matthew 27:43), the pierced hands and feet (Psalm 22:16), the bones out of joint, the tongue cleaving to the jaws, and the parting of garments with lots cast for the vesture (Psalm 22:18; John 19:24). The standard critical treatment reduces these to a sufferer’s generic lament that the evangelists later mined for correspondences. That explanation must account for a psalm written centuries before crucifixion was practised, describing pierced hands and feet and a division of clothing by lot, and closing with a declaration to a people yet unborn. This dictionary holds predictive prophecy as prophecy, and treats the Gospels’ use of the psalm as identification rather than invention.

Psalm 11 and Psalm 64 belong together as a pair on the manner of malice. The wicked prepare, string the arrow, and shoot privily — concealment is part of the method, and the whole force of Psalm 11 is that the righteous man is advised to flee and answers that he trusts in the LORD. God’s response in Psalm 64 uses the same weapon and reverses the timing: they were secret, He is sudden. The pattern is worth holding on to when a believer is under a campaign he cannot see the shape of. Scripture does not promise the arrows will miss; it says the LORD is in His holy temple, His eyes behold, His eyelids try the children of men (Psalm 11:4), and the outcome is His to arrange.
roots_summary: Hebrew yarah (H3384), to shoot or cast, the same root that gives torah, teaching aimed at a mark; chets (H2671), an arrow; pathar (H6362), to open, of the lip.
roots_lines: Hebrew yarah (H3384) — to cast or shoot; the root also of torah, instruction, as an arrow aimed at a target.
Hebrew chets (H2671) — an arrow; God shall shoot at them with an arrow (Psalm 64:7).
Hebrew pathar (H6362) — to open or separate; they shoot out the lip, a gesture of derision (Psalm 22:7).
Hebrew sethar (H5643) — secrecy, concealment; privily shoot at the upright in heart (Psalm 11:2).
Hebrew nua (H5128) — to shake or wag; they shake the head (Psalm 22:7).
usage: That they may privily shoot at the upright in heart (Psalm 11:2) — preparation, concealment, a specific target.
But God shall shoot at them with an arrow; suddenly shall they be wounded (Psalm 64:7) — they were secret; He is sudden.
They shoot out the lip, they shake the head (Psalm 22:7) — the gesture recorded again at Calvary.

etymology: From Anglo-Saxon plegan, to exercise, to sport, to play an instrument. Webster 1828: to do something not as a task but for pleasure; to sport; to perform on an instrument. Exodus uses it for what Israel did at the calf, and David for what he did before the ark.
biblical_def: The word does duty for three quite different things, and the difference is everything. At Sinai it names the golden-calf revelry: they rose up early on the morrow, and offered burnt offerings, and brought peace offerings; and the people sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play (Exodus 32:6) — the verb is a euphemism, and Paul cites this verse when warning the Corinthians against idolatry (1 Corinthians 10:7). It names David’s music, prescribed as a remedy for Saul: seek out a man, who is a cunning player on an harp... he shall play with his hand, and thou shalt be well (1 Samuel 16:16). And it names David’s answer to a wife who despised his dancing before the ark: It was before the LORD, which chose me before thy father... therefore will I play before the LORD (2 Samuel 6:21). Zechariah puts the word in his picture of a restored city, and it is one of the loveliest verses in the prophets: the streets of the city shall be full of boys and girls playing in the streets thereof (Zechariah 8:5).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PLAY as to do something not as a task or for profit, but for amusement; to sport; to frolic; also, to perform on an instrument of music; to act a part on the stage.
webster_full: PLAY, v.i. — To do something not as a task, but for pleasure; to sport; to frolic.
To perform on an instrument of music; as, to play on a harp.
To act a part on the stage; to represent a character.
To move irregularly or with freedom; as, the light plays on the water.
Anglo-Saxon plegan, to exercise, to play; the noun plega, sport or game.
scriptures: Exodus 32:6
And they rose up early on the morrow, and offered burnt offerings, and brought peace offerings; and the people sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play.
1 Samuel 16:16

Let our lord now command thy servants, which are before thee, to seek out a man, who is a cunning player on an harp: and it shall come to pass, when the evil spirit from God is upon thee, that he shall play with his hand, and thou shalt be well.
2 Samuel 6:21

And David said unto Michal, It was before the LORD, which chose me before thy father, and before all his house, to appoint me ruler over the people of the LORD, over Israel: therefore will I play before the LORD.
Zechariah 8:5
And the streets of the city shall be full of boys and girls playing in the streets thereof.
corruption_summary: Exodus 32 and 2 Samuel 6 are both scenes of exuberant religious activity, and the difference between them is not intensity but whether God appointed it.
corruption_paragraphs: Israel at the calf offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, ate, drank, and rose up to play; David before the ark danced with all his might. Both are loud, physical and joyful, and one is idolatry while the other is worship. The difference is not the temperature but the warrant: the calf was a form of devotion Israel devised, while David was bringing the ark to the place God had chosen — though even David had to learn the manner of it, since Uzzah had died on the first attempt when the ark was carried on a cart instead of by the Levites (2 Samuel 6:6-7; 1 Chronicles 15:13). This is the regulative principle stated by two narratives: what God commands is required, and what He has not commanded is not permitted, and sincerity does not convert the second into the first.

Michal’s contempt and David’s answer are worth keeping in view when the argument runs the other way. She despised him for uncovering himself before the handmaids; he replied that it was before the LORD, and that he would be yet more vile in his own sight. Reverence in Scripture does not require a certain temperature of manner, and the assumption that dignity is the same thing as godliness is a cultural preference and not a biblical rule. What Scripture regulates is the content and warrant of worship, not the volume. Zechariah 8:5 belongs here too, as the corrective to a religion that has no room for ordinary gladness: God’s picture of a restored Jerusalem includes old men with staves and streets full of children playing.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsachaq (H6711), to laugh, sport, or play, with a euphemistic sense; sachaq (H7832), to laugh or play; nagan (H5059), to play a stringed instrument; Greek paizo (G3815), to play.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsachaq (H6711) — to laugh or sport, often with a sexual overtone; rose up to play (Exodus 32:6).
Greek paizo (G3815) — to play; Paul’s rendering when he quotes Exodus 32:6 in 1 Corinthians 10:7.
Hebrew nagan (H5059) — to touch or play a stringed instrument; a cunning player on an harp (1 Samuel 16:16).
Hebrew sachaq (H7832) — to laugh, to play, to dance; David before the LORD (2 Samuel 6:21).
Hebrew rechob (H7339) — a broad open place, a street; where the children play in Zechariah 8:5.
usage: The people sat down to eat and to drink, and rose up to play (Exodus 32:6) — a euphemism, and Paul cites it against idolatry.
Therefore will I play before the LORD (2 Samuel 6:21) — David’s answer to a wife who despised his dancing.
Boys and girls playing in the streets thereof (Zechariah 8:5) — God’s own picture of a restored city.

etymology: From Old Norse illr, bad, evil. Webster 1828: bad or evil, in a general sense; contrary to good. In the Authorized Version it usually means evil rather than unwell, and Paul uses it for what love never does.
biblical_def: The word in the Authorized Version means evil rather than sick, and Paul’s use of it is the summary of the second table of the law: Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law (Romans 13:10). The definition is negative and it is exact — the commandments Paul has just listed are prohibitions, and love keeps them all by never working harm. Isaiah pronounces the wicked man’s outcome with the same word: Woe unto the wicked! it shall be ill with him: for the reward of his hands shall be given him (Isaiah 3:11). The Psalter records a case in which the ill fell on a righteous man because of others: They angered him also at the waters of strife, so that it went ill with Moses for their sakes (Psalm 106:32) — Moses spoke unadvisedly with his lips and was barred from the land. And Jacob uses it of a family’s misjudgment: Wherefore dealt ye so ill with me, as to tell the man whether ye had yet a brother? (Genesis 43:6).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ILL as bad or evil, in a general sense; contrary to good; producing evil; unfortunate; and as a noun, wickedness, misfortune, or misery.
webster_full: ILL, a. — Bad or evil, in a general sense; contrary to good, physical or moral.
Producing evil or misfortune; as an ill omen.
Cross; crabbed; surly; peevish; as ill nature, ill temper.
ILL, n. — Wickedness; depravity; evil; also misfortune, calamity, misery.
Old Norse illr, bad; the sense of unwell is later English.
scriptures: Romans 13:10
Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law.
Isaiah 3:11
Woe unto the wicked! it shall be ill with him: for the reward of his hands shall be given him.
Psalm 106:32
They angered him also at the waters of strife, so that it went ill with Moses for their sakes:
Genesis 43:6
And Israel said, Wherefore dealt ye so ill with me, as to tell the man whether ye had yet a brother?
corruption_summary: Romans 13:10 defines love as fulfilling the law, which is the exact reverse of the modern claim that love overrides the law wherever the two appear to conflict.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul’s sentence runs in the opposite direction from its most common modern use. Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law — love fulfils the commandments, and the commandments define what love looks like. He has just listed them: thou shalt not commit adultery, thou shalt not kill, thou shalt not steal, thou shalt not bear false witness, thou shalt not covet. The argument that love permits what the law forbids, wherever a relationship seems loving enough, requires the verse to mean that love replaces the law; it says love keeps it. This is the answer to the formula that makes affection self-authenticating and the appeal that treats any prohibition as unloving by definition. Our Lord makes the same connection: If ye love me, keep my commandments (John 14:15).

Psalm 106:32 is a sober text about consequences that fall on a faithful man through the sin of others. It went ill with Moses at Meribah — he was provoked, spoke unadvisedly with his lips, struck the rock, and was barred from the land he had spent forty years walking toward. Numbers 20 does not excuse him and the psalm does not either; but it does record that the people angered him and that the ill came for their sakes. Two things follow. Provocation does not remove responsibility — God held Moses to the standard of a leader who represents Him before the congregation. And the consequences of a moment can be permanent even where the sin is forgiven, which is why Moses is nonetheless on the mount of transfiguration, in the land, with Christ.
roots_summary: Greek kakos (G2556), bad, evil; Hebrew ra (H7451), evil, bad, harmful; yara (H3415), to be displeasing or grievous.
roots_lines: Greek kakos (G2556) — bad, evil, harmful; love worketh no ill (Romans 13:10).
Greek pleroma (G4138) — fulness, that which fills up; love is the fulfilling of the law (Romans 13:10).
Hebrew ra (H7451) — evil, bad, calamitous; it shall be ill with him (Isaiah 3:11).
Hebrew yara (H3415) — to be evil or displeasing; it went ill with Moses (Psalm 106:32).
Hebrew gemul (H1576) — a recompense or reward; the reward of his hands shall be given him (Isaiah 3:11).
usage: Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law (Romans 13:10) — love keeps the commandments, it does not replace them.
Woe unto the wicked! it shall be ill with him (Isaiah 3:11) — the recompense is his own hands’ work returned.
It went ill with Moses for their sakes (Psalm 106:32) — provocation real, and responsibility undiminished.

etymology: Superlative of old, from Anglo-Saxon ieldesta. Webster 1828: oldest; that was born before others. In two narratives the eldest is where a search or a conviction begins, and in both the order is significant.
biblical_def: Joseph’s steward searches the sacks in a sequence that builds suspense and proves a point: he searched, and began at the eldest, and left at the youngest: and the cup was found in Benjamin's sack (Genesis 44:12). Ten sacks are opened and cleared before the last one damns the brother Jacob could least spare, and the whole test is designed to see whether these men will now abandon a favoured younger son as they once abandoned Joseph. They do not; Judah offers himself instead. John records a different search conducted by conscience, and it moves in the same direction: they which heard it, being convicted by their own conscience, went out one by one, beginning at the eldest, even unto the last: and Jesus was left alone, and the woman standing in the midst (John 8:9). The oldest went first, having most to remember. Samuel records the three eldest sons of Jesse following Saul to the battle while the youngest kept sheep (1 Samuel 17:13), and Job’s children were feasting in their eldest brother’s house when the messengers came (Job 1:13).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ELDEST as oldest; most advanced in age; that was born before others; and of a family, the first-born.
webster_full: ELDEST, a. — Oldest; most advanced in age; that was born before others.
ELDER, a. — Older; having lived a longer time; prior in origin.
ELDER, n. — One who is older; an officer in the church, a presbyter.
ELDERSHIP, n. — Seniority; also the office of an elder.
Anglo-Saxon ieldesta, superlative of eald, old.
scriptures: Genesis 44:12
And he searched, and began at the eldest, and left at the youngest: and the cup was found in Benjamin's sack.
John 8:9
And they which heard it, being convicted by their own conscience, went out one by one, beginning at the eldest, even unto the last: and Jesus was left alone, and the woman standing in the midst.
1 Samuel 17:13

And the three eldest sons of Jesse went and followed Saul to the battle: and the names of his three sons that went to the battle were Eliab the firstborn, and next unto him Abinadab, and the third Shammah.
Job 1:13
And there was a day when his sons and his daughters were eating and drinking wine in their eldest brother's house:
corruption_summary: John 8:9 shows conscience working without a word of accusation from Christ, which the popular use of the passage as a rule against all moral judgment entirely inverts.
corruption_paragraphs: He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her is probably the most cited verse in the modern world and one of the least understood. It is not a prohibition of moral judgment: the same Christ, in the same paragraph, tells the woman go, and sin no more — naming what she had done as sin and requiring it to stop. What He refuses is the right of these particular men, who had brought the woman without the man and used her as bait for a trap, to execute a sentence they had no standing to execute. Conscience did the rest, and it began at the eldest, who had most to remember. To read the verse as forbidding all moral assessment one must delete the last sentence of the story, and it is generally deleted.

Genesis 44 is worth reading as the test it is. Joseph places his cup in Benjamin’s sack and has the search begin at the eldest, so that ten brothers are cleared in turn and the youngest — the son of Rachel, his father’s favourite, exactly the position Joseph himself had occupied — is left holding the evidence. The brothers are being offered the same choice they made years earlier, with every incentive to take it: they could leave Benjamin and go home. Instead they rend their clothes and return, and Judah, who had proposed selling Joseph, offers himself as bondman in the boy’s place. That is what genuine repentance looks like in Scripture: not remorse expressed, but the same temptation refused in the same circumstances.
roots_summary: Hebrew gadol (H1419), great, and so eldest; bekor (H1060), firstborn; Greek presbuteros (G4245), older, an elder.
roots_lines: Hebrew gadol (H1419) — great, and by extension the eldest; began at the eldest (Genesis 44:12).
Hebrew bekor (H1060) — the firstborn, with the rights of the birthright; Eliab in 1 Samuel 17:13.
Greek presbuteros (G4245) — older, elder; beginning at the eldest (John 8:9) and the church office of elder.
Greek suneidesis (G4893) — conscience, joint-knowledge; what convicted the accusers (John 8:9).
Hebrew qaton (H6996) — small, young, least; left at the youngest (Genesis 44:12).
usage: He searched, and began at the eldest, and left at the youngest (Genesis 44:12) — a sequence designed to isolate the favoured son.
Being convicted by their own conscience, went out one by one, beginning at the eldest (John 8:9) — the oldest had most to remember.
The three eldest sons of Jesse went and followed Saul to the battle (1 Samuel 17:13) — and the youngest kept sheep.

etymology: From Anglo-Saxon dropa, a small globule of liquid. Webster 1828: a small portion of any fluid falling at once; a very small quantity. Moses asks that his teaching fall like rain, and Isaiah weighs the nations as a drop of a bucket.
biblical_def: Moses opens his final song with a request about the manner of his words: My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew, as the small rain upon the tender herb, and as the showers upon the grass (Deuteronomy 32:2). Four figures, and all of them gradual — rain, dew, small rain, showers. Doctrine that arrives as a flood runs off; doctrine that drops soaks in, which is an argument for patient and repeated teaching rather than for one overwhelming exposure. Elihu describes the mechanism as God’s: Which the clouds do drop and distil upon man abundantly (Job 36:28). Amos uses the word for a fertility so extravagant it is comic: the mountains shall drop sweet wine, and all the hills shall melt (Amos 9:13), in a passage where the plowman overtakes the reaper because the harvest has not finished before the next sowing begins. And Isaiah uses a single drop to state the proportion between God and the nations: Behold, the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance (Isaiah 40:15).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DROP as a small portion of any fluid which falls at once; a globule; a very small quantity of liquid; and as a verb, to distil, to let fall in drops.
webster_full: DROP, n. — A small portion of any fluid which falls at once, or a globule.
A very small quantity of liquid; as, a drop of water.
An earring, or a hanging ornament of similar shape.
DROP, v.i. — To distil; to fall in small portions or globules; to let fall.
Anglo-Saxon dropa, a drop; the verb dropian, to fall in drops.
scriptures: Deuteronomy 32:2
My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew, as the small rain upon the tender herb, and as the showers upon the grass:
Which the clouds do drop and distil upon man abundantly.
Amos 9:13

Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that the plowman shall overtake the reaper, and the treader of grapes him that soweth seed; and the mountains shall drop sweet wine, and all the hills shall melt.
Isaiah 40:15
Behold, the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance: behold, he taketh up the isles as a very little thing.
corruption_summary: Deuteronomy 32:2 makes gradual, repeated teaching the model for doctrine, which is a direct rebuke to a preaching culture organized around the single memorable event.
corruption_paragraphs: Every figure in Moses’s opening request is slow: rain, dew, small rain on tender herb, showers on grass. None of them is a flood, and the reason is agricultural — a downpour on dry ground runs off, while small rain soaks in. Applied to teaching, this argues for the ordinary means the Reformed tradition has always emphasized: consecutive exposition week upon week, catechizing of children, family worship, the same truths returned to until they are in the ground. It is a rebuke to a model built on the conference, the campaign, and the sermon designed to be unforgettable. Nothing in Scripture forbids a memorable sermon; what it denies is that the memorable event is how doctrine gets into a people. Moses had forty years of evidence for the point he was making.

Isaiah 40:15 supplies the proportion that governs Christian political sanity. The nations — not one weak nation but the nations — are a drop hanging on the rim of a bucket and the fine dust on a balance pan, too small to move the scale. This is said in a chapter that also has God holding the seas in His palm and calling the stars by name. Two errors are cut off at once. The first is the despair that reads the headlines and concludes that God’s cause is in danger; the second is the idolatry that invests a nation or a party with ultimate weight, which is the same error in a hopeful key. The lordship of Christ over every sphere does not make any earthly sphere weigh more than a drop before Him.
roots_summary: Hebrew araph (H6201), to drip or drop; nataph (H5197), to drop or distil, used of prophesying; mar (H4752), a drop; zaqaq (H2212), to distil or refine.
roots_lines: Hebrew araph (H6201) — to drip or drop; my doctrine shall drop as the rain (Deuteronomy 32:2).
Hebrew nataph (H5197) — to drop or distil; used both of rain and, idiomatically, of prophesying (Amos 7:16).
Hebrew zaqaq (H2212) — to strain or distil; the clouds do drop and distil (Job 36:28).
Hebrew mar (H4752) — a drop; the nations are as a drop of a bucket (Isaiah 40:15).
Hebrew leqach (H3948) — doctrine, what is received or taken in; the subject of Deuteronomy 32:2.
usage: My doctrine shall drop as the rain (Deuteronomy 32:2) — four figures, all of them gradual.
The mountains shall drop sweet wine (Amos 9:13) — an extravagance in which harvest overtakes sowing.
The nations are as a drop of a bucket (Isaiah 40:15) — too small to move the scale.
